stable-summary: Claude Code skills are directories centered on SKILL.md instructions and frontmatter. Official docs cover direct /skill-name invocation, autonomous skill invocation based on description, invocation controls including disable-model-invocation, visibility controls, allowed-tools permission grants while active, and argument handling. For cog consumers, this is the official source for Claude skill authoring and invocation behavior.

Claude Code commands are slash-prefixed controls recognized at the start of a message, with trailing text passed as arguments. Skill and custom-command slash invocation expands before reaching Claude; UserPromptExpansion hooks cover that direct invocation path and can block or add context, while PreToolUse only covers model-initiated Skill tool calls. Consumers that govern skills must account for both direct slash invocation and model-selected invocation.

Claude Code plan mode is the official mode for reviewing proposed changes before disk writes. It can be started with claude --permission-mode plan, toggled with Shift+Tab, or entered with /plan during a session. Official docs describe this as a read-and-plan flow that waits for approval before edits, matching cog's requirement that plan-emitting Claude skills must not run inside Claude's read-only plan mode.

Claude Code configuration spans managed, user, project, and local scopes, with CLI flags overriding some session behavior. Relevant controls include disabling slash commands and skills for a session, disallowed tool rules, settings-driven skill visibility, and hooks that provide deterministic lifecycle controls. cog skill and executor guidance should treat these runtime controls as external policy inputs rather than reimplementing them in skill prose.

Official Codex docs define non-interactive automation through codex exec. Continuing a non-interactive run uses the resume subcommand under exec, such as codex exec resume --last with a follow-up prompt or codex exec resume <SESSION_ID>; interactive sessions also have top-level codex resume. Resumed runs retain prior transcript, plan history, and approvals, so cog wrappers should keep direct native resume construction centralized.

Official Codex configuration separates sandbox access from approval prompting. The documented sandbox modes include read-only, workspace-write, and danger-full-access, with permission profiles such as :read-only, :workspace, and :danger-full-access. approval_policy controls when Codex pauses for approvals, and granular approvals include sandbox escalation, rules, MCP elicitations, request_permissions, and skill approval. Command rules can allow, prompt, or forbid matched command prefixes.

Official Codex configuration uses model_reasoning_effort for reasoning effort. The core accepted values are minimal, low, medium, and high, with xhigh documented as model-dependent in current guidance. OpenAI guidance frames low as suitable for faster bounded tasks and medium or high for more complex work. Cross-checked against /workspaces/cog/docs/reference/model-effort-policy.md and found consistent (no divergence): cog routes effort selection through its provider policy rather than hard-coding task-specific native flags in skills, so the official effort values inform but do not override the repo policy.

Official Codex docs define skills as directories with required SKILL.md files and optional scripts, references, assets, and agent metadata. SKILL.md must include name and description. Codex can activate skills explicitly through /skills or $-mentions (e.g. typing $ to mention a skill, such as $skill-creator), or implicitly when the task matches the description. Codex also reads AGENTS.md guidance before work and layers global and project instructions into the prompt, so skill behavior and repository instructions are distinct but complementary inputs.

Divergence (frontmatter requiredness + key allowlist), cog SoT vs official Claude Code skill docs. (1) Required keys: official docs mark ALL frontmatter fields optional - name is Required=No (defaults to the directory name) and description is Required=Recommended (falls back to the first markdown paragraph) - whereas /workspaces/cog/docs/reference/skill-contract.md requires BOTH name and description in every SKILL.md. The repo contract is therefore stricter on required keys, not in agreement with the Claude runtime. (2) Key allowlist: the official docs enumerate a fixed set of optional supported fields (name, description, when_to_use, argument-hint, arguments, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, allowed-tools, disallowed-tools, model, effort, context, agent, hooks, paths, shell) and do not document behavior for unknown keys; cog's skill-lint separately enforces its own fixed frontmatter-key allowlist and rejects keys outside it. Practical impact: cog's required-key strictness and its allowlist are local repository governance rules layered on top of the official spec; future skill authors should preserve the stricter repo contract unless an ADR changes it.

Best-practice planning patterns for coding agents separate exploration and planning from implementation. Anthropic recommends using plan mode for non-trivial tasks so the agent can read files, answer questions, and produce a plan before editing; its power-user guidance further treats plan refinement as the investment that lets implementation proceed in one focused pass. For cog plan skills, this supports a read/research-first planner contract, explicit reviewable plan output, and a clean handoff from plan emission to execution.

Plan-review skills map cleanly to evaluator-optimizer and reflect-refine workflows: one model or agent produces an artifact, while a separate evaluator applies a rubric or critique prompt and returns actionable feedback before acceptance. Anthropic and AWS both describe this as a feedback-control pattern for iterative improvement. For cog review-plan-* skills, this supports adversarial plan review, explicit acceptance criteria, structured critique, and a bounded return to the planner or executor rather than silent self-approval.

sources.title: A practical guide to building agents

stable-summary: Executor and handoff patterns should choose orchestration deliberately. OpenAI distinguishes manager-style agents-as-tools, where a central agent stays responsible for the final answer while specialists act as tools, from decentralized handoffs, where execution transfers to another agent. OpenAI's Agents SDK also frames agents as instruction-bearing units with tools, handoffs, guardrails, and structured outputs. For cog executor skills, this supports keeping a single executor responsible for final session state unless an explicit handoff boundary is required, and returning structured results across orchestration boundaries.

Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym
Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
MAGICoRe: Multi-Agent, Iterative, Coarse-to-Fine Refinement for Reasoning

stable-summary: Empirical synthesis on two orchestration patterns for AI plan/artifact generation: (a) one model generates and a SEPARATE model reviews/critiques (generator-reviewer, self-refine, evaluator-optimizer), versus (b) multiple models generate full candidates independently in parallel and an orchestrator selects or synthesizes the best (parallel sampling, best-of-N, aggregation). The deciding variable is reviewer/verifier reliability, not the pattern itself. Evidence: intrinsic self-correction without an external signal is unreliable and can DEGRADE reasoning quality (Huang et al., DeepMind, 2310.01798); LLM-as-judge shows strong position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, so a reviewer should be a DIFFERENT model grounded in a rubric, tests, or tools (Zheng et al., MT-Bench, 2306.05685); self-refine helps mainly on structured refinement tasks with clear criteria (Madaan et al., 2303.17651). Parallel generation plus selection is robust when the selector is decent, and cross-model diversity is the main value driver (Mixture-of-Agents 2406.04692; multiagent debate 2305.14325, though much of debate's measured gain reduces to majority voting); repeated sampling exposes large latent upside gated by selection quality (Large Language Monkeys 2407.21787; SWE-Gym 2412.21139); self-consistency / majority voting is reliable where a numeric reward is not (Wang et al., 2203.11171). The strongest pattern is HYBRID: sample diverse candidates in parallel, aggregate, then selectively apply a reviewer gate where concrete artifacts and external checks make the reviewer trustworthy (MAGICORE 2409.12147). Practical defaults for skill design: prefer parallel-generate-then-synthesize for high-stakes, open-ended artifact creation that lacks a deterministic verifier; use a cross-model generator-to-reviewer gate where the reviewer has tests, repo constraints, or an explicit rubric; avoid rubric-free same-model self-critique on hard tasks; keep generator and reviewer on different models or differently-prompted roles; and validate that any review loop measurably improves output rather than assuming it does.

How to write a good spec

stable-summary: Best practices for authoring implementation plans consumed by AI coding agents converge across Anthropic (Claude Code best practices; context engineering), GitHub Spec Kit, AWS Kiro, and spec-driven-development writing (BrainGrid, Osmani, Galileo). Load-bearing principles: concrete-over-abstract (name exact files/commands/signals); machine-checkable acceptance criteria in Given-When-Then/EARS shape; requirement-to-task traceability via R-IDs; an end-to-end verification gate per plan; explicit scope/out-of-scope to prevent drift; right-size to one session and split large work into separate self-contained plans rather than summarizing. Lean governs format, never depth. Captured as the single cog SoT at skill-refs/plan-quality/plan-quality-principles.md (resolved via cog skill-refs path).
Reviewed markdown pre-commit formatting policy; dprint remains the single markdown formatter and markdown.textWrap="never" is the shipped default for one physical line per soft-wrapped paragraph.
